title: AI for Self-Help and Legal Aid at the Innovations in Technology Conference — full episode transcript
pub: Talk Justice, Legal Services Corporation / Legal Talk Network
author: Scheree Gilchrist · Conor Malloy · Quinten Steenhuis

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source endorses human-centred augmentation and reports law students’ anxiety about AI’s career effects, but it does not assess whether automation is removing apprenticeship work, creating a verification-expertise paradox, or requiring reconstructed associate training. Its teaching response is not described in the supplied excerpt.
qs: Cat Moon:  So I love that particular example, Quentin, because I’m really spending a lot of time thinking and focusing on how we use AI to give us super human powers and how we keep human users at the center of this work, that it’s not about robots.

I teach a course called AI and law practice and law students are no different than practicing lawyers in terms of their curiosity mixed with fear, mixed with a little bit of apprehension about this technology and the impact it’s going to have on their future careers.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source accepts the value of task-specific legal workflows and materially extends the cluster by applying them to statewide legal-aid intake, including pre-screening, referral and eligibility processing, while outlining a low-cost path from general-model experiments to a client-facing application. Its claims remain prospective and do not establish human verification, reliability or measured outcomes.
qs: So that is sort of low hanging fruit for us to use AI to do some of that pre-screening, to filter out people who don’t necessarily need to be in our process because they may not be eligible or it’s not the right sort of help for them and redirect ’em to the best sort of help.

And then you take that, you’ve tried it a few times, you can move it into the open AI playground, that’s their more backend developer interface and you can, it will generate some of the code for you and you can start to test it and build around it and get something that actually does something real in the real world.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core technology-competence and confidentiality framework, then materially develops its governance implications: legal organisations should integrate AI into existing privacy and cybersecurity controls rather than automatically create separate restrictive policies. It also distinguishes deployment models by asserted data use, although its broad safety comparison is less cautious than the cluster’s lifecycle, fact-specific approach.
qs: We’re redefining them to include AI and how it should be used, but I don’t think we need to necessarily jump to creating AI policies that restrict the opportunities that come with using the tools.
But that assumes that folks understand the technology and are proceeding ethically to figure out how to use it.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The panel accepts the cluster’s human-led, selective-deployment proposition and materially extends it for legal aid and self-help: use client-centred design, vetted organisational content, purpose-built tools, education and institutional support rather than uncontrolled standalone AI. It also identifies access-specific constraints—including cost, UPL rules, privacy and moderation—while treating several proposed safeguards as aspirational rather than proven.
qs: Cat Moon:  So I hear the human centeredness popping up again and again and I’m reminded that ultimately humans are going to remain at the center of what we decide to do with this technology.
We need to feed the chatbot with our own content that’s safe and that’s moderated.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s balanced position: AI may expand legal-service delivery, but direct users can misunderstand or over-rely on its outputs, while cost and implementation barriers may leave legal-aid clients behind. Its proposed responses—client education, affordable adoption and partnerships—align with supervised, equitable deployment rather than unrestricted substitution for lawyers.
qs: So I think part of it is we have an obligation as legal services providers to ensure that our client communities are educated and understand these tools and they can use it effectively.

So if we don’t figure out a way to adopt it or create partnerships that will allow us to integrate it into our work without expending resources that we don’t have that our clients and our practice areas might get left behind.

st.t: Justice augmentation: Activity exceeds proven access gains
st.an: Moon supports the cluster’s broad access-to-justice framing by predicting that people will use AI independently to meet needs and solve problems. However, the source offers a behavioural prediction rather than evidence of improved legal access, outcomes or reliable self-help, and it does not address preserving human legal relationships.
qs: They’re going to take the electricity of AI and they’re going to figure out how to meet their needs and solve their problems.
And that’s going to happen whether anyone in this room does a damn thing or not to help them do this.

st.t: Justice capacity: AI potential requires deliberate implementation
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s urgency and access-to-justice framing by predicting that the public will use AI for legal needs regardless of professional involvement. It does not, however, provide evidence of improved access or explain the deliberate implementation, safeguards or evaluation needed to make that use effective and safe.
qs: They’re going to take the electricity of AI and they’re going to figure out how to meet their needs and solve their problems.
And that’s going to happen whether anyone in this room does a damn thing or not to help them do this.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source accepts AI’s potential to broaden meaningful legal help while arguing that uptake alone is insufficient. It stresses client education, affordable integration and partnerships to prevent legal-aid providers and their clients from falling behind; its broader-service forecast remains qualified and speculative.
qs: So I think part of it is we have an obligation as legal services providers to ensure that our client communities are educated and understand these tools and they can use it effectively.

So if we don’t figure out a way to adopt it or create partnerships that will allow us to integrate it into our work without expending resources that we don’t have that our clients and our practice areas might get left behind.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s caution against treating demonstrations or generated output as proof of reliable delivery. It presents Copilot as useful for producing a first draft while explicitly noting the recommendation lacks firsthand testing and that output quality, particularly aesthetics, remains limited. It does not materially develop the cluster’s legal-service implementation, verification or evaluation framework.
qs: I haven’t tried it yet, but I’ve seen some pretty cool demos.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source endorses bounded, human-centred augmentation: generative AI can streamline guided legal interviews, but users retain review and approval rather than relying on autonomous output. It also aligns this workflow with improving access to legal help, while offering no evidence on measured productivity gains or verification costs.
qs: These are all uses where the user gets to review and approve what they’re saying.
It’s about how we are leveraging technology to help humans get legal help do our work better.

kp.k: Unmet demand drives legal aid beyond one-to-one representation
kp.d: Scheree Gilchrist reports that Legal Aid of North Carolina covers all 100 counties, receives about 400,000 helpline contacts annually and serves about 55,000 people annually, with 450 staff members including 250 attorneys. She argues that its longstanding one-to-one attorney model cannot meet demand; its innovation lab seeks scalable delivery rather than simply expanding individual representation.
qs: We have about 400,000 people that contact our helpline every year and we serve about 55,000 people annually.
we have 450 staff members, 250 attorneys
we were looking at solutions to allow us to move from one to one to one to 10, one to a hundred, one to a thousand.

kp.k: AI could streamline intake, eligibility screening and referrals
kp.d: Gilchrist describes prospective AI applications to North Carolina's centralized intake system: pre-screening and redirecting unsuitable or ineligible applicants, automating eligibility screening, and potentially adding translation and transcription. These are proposed responses to client frustration and slow access, not measured improvements.
qs: there’s a lot of frustration around how people interact with legal aid and how quickly they can get service.

use AI to do some of that pre-screening, to filter out people who don’t necessarily need to be in our process because they may not be eligible or it’s not the right sort of help for them and redirect ’em to the best sort of help.
maybe even language translation and even transcription services

kp.k: Human-reviewed code generation augments existing document automation
kp.d: Quinten Steenhuis describes using generative AI to draft code for the lab's doc assemble work, followed by human editing, refinement and review before client exposure. He presents this as a comparatively safe augmentation strategy. He also says chat experimentation and the OpenAI playground lower iteration costs, while later acknowledging that production deployment can still require an engineering team.
qs: we’ve focused quite a lot on augmentation
we’re using it to build first drafts of the code that we can then edit and improve
nothing goes out into the world from that. That’s actually touched by the client without a human looking it over and reviewing it and making sure it’s right.
It takes an engineering team.

kp.k: Narrative intake can improve guided interviews without autonomous output
kp.d: Steenhuis proposes retaining carefully designed interview questions while letting users first tell their stories, extracting relevant information into the interview and avoiding repeated questions. His motivation includes feedback from an eviction-defense tool user who felt unable to express the most important issue. He emphasizes user review and approval rather than sending unreviewed AI-generated material into the world.
qs: We don’t want to have the generative AI making those every time.
tell us your whole story. We’re going to see what in there we can use and plug into the right place through the rest of the guided interview flow.
These are all uses where the user gets to review and approve what they’re saying.

kp.k: AI complements existing systems and human-centered service design
kp.d: Gilchrist emphasizes designing around clients' needs and experiences. Host Cat Moon frames generative AI as an additional layer in existing technology stacks rather than a replacement for prior investment, potentially making interactions more human by allowing users to tell stories that become usable in legal processes.
qs: We start with our clients, we develop solutions for our clients.
Part of the puzzle we’re putting together here is how does this fit together with stuff we’re already doing?
generative AI has come along to add an additional layer and that layer actually might give a more human touch to so many of the things that we’re doing.

kp.k: Reliable legal applications require datasets and rigorous evaluation
kp.d: Steenhuis recommends collecting community-relevant legal questions and good answers, testing reliability beyond a few trials, and potentially improving outputs through fine-tuning and prompting. He stresses probabilistic variability. Conor Malloy separately warns that fluent language can conceal incompetence; his suggestion that tipping a chatbot improves outcomes is presented as personal experience, not a systematic finding.
qs: how do we know if they’re good for answering the legal questions of the people that are our community?
we need to have some more rigorous way to know they’re going to be reliable.
it’s a probability engine, it’s not a calculator, it’s not going to give the exact same result.
it’s this eloquent incompetence that these things are just masters of language and that’s all they know.

kp.k: Connectivity and moderation can exclude vulnerable users
kp.d: Steenhuis identifies two inclusion problems: basic connectivity barriers, illustrated by another conference speaker's account of people seeking high ground to access remote hearings, and moderation systems that block responses to upsetting client circumstances. He argues that legal-help tools must handle bad news and difficult facts, and worries that alternative engines could leave clients with lower-quality solutions; his preference for GPT-4 is a contemporaneous judgment.
qs: they had to go to the top of the highest peak to be able to get cell reception to be able to call in for their basic hearings.
the facts, the situations that our clients are dealing with are too upsetting for open AI to be able to respond to it.
We don’t want people to be restricted from using these tools because their situations have some Flagg that raises a concern from OpenAI.

kp.k: Client adoption creates an education imperative for providers
kp.d: Gilchrist asserts that clients already use AI and recommends education about prompting and how generative AI works to avoid harmful reliance when preparing pro se pleadings. Moon predicts public use for legal problem-solving will continue regardless of professional participation, arguing that providers should engage intentionally and quickly rather than assume control over adoption.
qs: we have an obligation as legal services providers to ensure that our client communities are educated and understand these tools and they can use it effectively.
they can then create a pro se pleading or something with that may not be as useful or helpful as they think.
people are just going to go to the tools

kp.k: Costs and regulation could widen the justice gap
kp.d: In her 2024 outlook, Gilchrist worries that fear surrounding fabricated cases and regulatory responses could chill beneficial uses, while costs could leave legal aid programs and their clients behind. She recommends partnerships to access and responsibly develop technology, and speculates that AI may redefine legal services beyond lawyer-only solutions. Malloy likewise identifies potential overregulation as a concern.
qs: Some of the regulatory work around AI and how it can be used, there might be a chilling effect on some of the opportunities.
a lot of legal aid programs perhaps won’t be able to purchase large language models or take advantage of some of the opportunities that it’ll create a wider gap.
it might force us to redefine what legal services actually means and perhaps force us to move away from a lawyer only solution

kp.k: Conversational tools may support empathy and preventive legal help
kp.d: Malloy predicts opportunities for conversational legal coaches that respond sensitively to different situations and help prevent problems upstream, supplementing professionals whose empathy can fluctuate. Gilchrist offers an internal testing anecdote from a website virtual assistant under development with Laroy: it responded constructively to criticism and directed users toward services. This supports the speakers' enthusiasm, not a measured finding about client outcomes.
qs: if we can open up that space to allow for this legal coach, and I think that’s where you might see things to kind of go upstream and be preventative about it
These things can express appropriate levels of empathy for certain types of situations that you’re experiencing.
we have a project with Laroy right now where we’re developing a virtual assistant for our website.
this is exactly what it should be saying and how it should respond to our clients.

kp.k: Productized tools could reduce engineering and subscription barriers
kp.d: Steenhuis reports Saam Harden's conference statement that there were already 1,600 custom legal GPTs, accessible through a $20 monthly subscription. He contrasts experimentation with the substantial engineering needed for a GPT-4 self-help chatbot at People's Law School. Looking a year ahead, he predicts off-the-shelf products that allow organizations to build vetted tools using their own content with less engineering effort.
qs: there’s already 1,600 custom GPTs for law if you go to the OpenAI GPT store, but you need to be a paying subscriber to access those $20 a month.
That was a big engineering project.
We need to feed the chatbot with our own content that’s safe and that’s moderated.
if I’m looking ahead at a year, we’re going to see some great off the shelf products that do that.

kp.k: Privacy safeguards motivate purpose-built and local AI tools
kp.d: Steenhuis asserts that, under the OpenAI policies he describes at the time, subscribed chat users who turn off history and users of backend API systems avoid training use of their data; he contrasts this with free ChatGPT and recommends purpose-built tools. Gilchrist expresses enthusiasm for local closed models as a way to eliminate fears around hallucinations, bias and confidentiality. These are speakers' policy interpretations and expectations, not independently demonstrated security or accuracy findings.
qs: they’re not using your data for training purposes if you have a subscription and you turn off history.
If you’ve built a system that uses the backend API that is built in, they’re not using your data for training purposes
the free chat GPT is different. It is going to use your data for training.

creating local closed LLMs that legal services programs can use so that some of the fears around hallucinations and bias and put in confidential information into these large language models can be eliminated.

kp.k: Existing professional duties should encompass AI use
kp.d: Gilchrist recommends adapting existing confidentiality, privacy and cybersecurity policies rather than creating restrictive standalone AI policies. Moon agrees and invokes technology competence under comment eight to Rule 1.1, treating understanding AI as an ethical responsibility. Her estimate that 42 states recognize an affirmative technology-competence duty is explicitly tentative.
qs: I think it’s just a matter of tweaking your policies.
I think 42 states I might be overstating, but most states now have an affirmative duty of technology competence for lawyers as an ethical obligation.
that assumes that folks understand the technology and are proceeding ethically to figure out how to use it.
I think it’s comment eight to rule 1.1, competence technology competence.

kp.k: UPL reform should enable safer access-to-justice tools
kp.d: Steenhuis advocates unauthorized-practice-of-law reform, criticizing variable and incoherent distinctions between legal advice and information. He argues against restricting vetted services when clients can otherwise use less-safe public tools, while recommending starting with non-advice tasks and discussing borderline uses with courts. His suggestion of possible safe harbor for free access-to-justice tools is tentative. Malloy stresses institutional support, education and the problems of standalone systems with uncontrolled outputs.
qs: I think we need UPL reform.
I don’t think that current unauthorized practice of law policy is coherent.
a lot of the things we can do don’t involve giving advice that really smooth and improve the client experience.
There’s probably some safe harbor that comes for our free access to justice solutions
When it stands on its own, that’s always going to be problematic, especially if you can’t control the outputs.

kp.k: Low-risk experimentation builds practical competence and client understanding
kp.d: Moon recommends internal, low-stakes experiments and having lawyers or students approach a client's problem as an uninformed user to learn both the tool and the client's experience. Practical suggestions include Malloy's email-tone checks, Gilchrist's plain-language rewriting without client information and translation, and Steenhuis's iterative editing. Steenhuis also suggests presentation generation with Microsoft Copilot, explicitly saying he has seen demonstrations but not tried it; Moon questions its aesthetics while accepting its first-draft value.
qs: very low stakes, very low risk of anything bad happening if the experiment doesn’t go really well
pretend that you are a person who you serve and sit down with the problem of one of your clients and try to use the tool to solve that problem.
was I passive aggressive in this email? Was I snarky?
You can take information that you’ve written without disclosing your client information and you can ask chat GPT or any of these models to just simplify it, write it at a fourth grade level for you.
I give it my first draft. I say what’s missing? How could I improve it? What questions would people ask?

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The interviewed speakers describe AI as a means of scaling legal aid, augmenting document automation and communication, and developing more accessible self-help services; they also predict changes in service delivery and warn of barriers to those changes.
pts.d: Scheree Gilchrist describes Legal Aid of North Carolina's exploration of AI for intake pre-screening, eligibility screening, redirection, translation and transcription, with the aim of serving more people than a one-to-one attorney model permits. She predicts AI might redefine legal services beyond lawyer-only solutions. Quinten Steenhuis reports using generative AI to draft code for document automation under human review and describes opportunities to extract information from users' narratives, populate guided interviews and avoid repetitive questions. He predicts off-the-shelf products will make it easier to build self-help chatbots using providers' own vetted content. Conor Malloy envisages conversational legal coaching that could provide preventative assistance and context-sensitive expressions of empathy, augmenting professionals' limitations rather than simply replacing lawyers. Gilchrist reports an internal website-assistant test that produced an appropriately empathetic response and directions to help. Malloy, Gilchrist and Steenhuis identify immediate uses in editing, tone checking, simplification and translation. Alongside these opportunities, Gilchrist and Malloy warn that regulation may inhibit development; Gilchrist warns that costs could leave legal aid clients and practice areas behind. Steenhuis says moderation can block responses to difficult client circumstances. Gilchrist expresses interest in local closed models as a way of eliminating fears about hallucinations, bias and confidential information; this is her expectation, not a reported measured result. The speakers' dominant framing is augmentation and supported self-help, with concerns about uncontrolled standalone outputs.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists principally of practitioners' development experience, organizational demand figures, an internal chatbot test and user feedback, rather than measured service improvements or formal performance benchmarks.
pts.d: Gilchrist grounds the scaling rationale in approximately 400,000 annual helpline contacts versus approximately 55,000 people served, with 450 staff including 250 attorneys; these are organizational context figures, not evidence of an AI-driven increase in service capacity. Her empathy claim includes a single reported internal test of a virtual assistant being developed with Laroy: after a negative comment, it apologized and explained Legal Aid of North Carolina's services with links. Steenhuis draws on the Lit Lab's code-drafting work and feedback from an eviction-defense tool user who felt unable to tell the most important part of their story. This supports the motivation for narrative intake, not a demonstrated outcome from that proposed AI workflow. He explicitly calls for datasets of relevant questions and answers and more rigorous reliability testing. His production-barrier discussion includes a secondhand account of the People's Law School chatbot project; his off-the-shelf product forecast draws on emerging products and conference exposure, not a quantified adoption forecast. Malloy cites everyday use for email tone feedback and analogizes conversational legal coaching to companion applications; he supplies no measured legal outcomes for such coaching. Gilchrist's predictions about costs, regulatory chilling and lawyer-only services are concerns and possibilities, without quantified forecasts. Steenhuis's presentation-generation suggestion rests on demonstrations he has seen, not personal testing. His statements about OpenAI privacy and relative model quality are assertions about the then-current tools, not independently established findings within this transcript.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The discussion distinguishes current experimentation and use from near-term predictions made in 2024, with benefits conditioned on verification, engineering capacity, responsible access and regulatory room.
pts.d: Current uses include code drafting, editing and email tone checking; intake changes and the website assistant are described as exploration or development, not as demonstrated statewide operational results. Steenhuis explicitly predicts easier off-the-shelf products within about a year of the 2024 conversation. Gilchrist identifies a potential immediate chilling effect from fear and regulation while treating broader redefinition of legal services as an uncertain future possibility. Steenhuis qualifies the ease of experimentation by acknowledging that production deployment still requires engineering. His code workflow requires human verification before client-facing use, and his narrative-interview proposals require user review and approval rather than directly sending unreviewed AI-generated material into the world. He calls for repeated reliability testing because outputs are probabilistic. Gilchrist conditions equitable adoption on affordable access and partnerships. Malloy conditions useful augmentation on professionals' willingness to use it and warns about standalone systems with uncontrollable outputs. Steenhuis recommends starting with tasks that do not give advice, advocates UPL reform and raises possible court consultation and safe harbor as avenues rather than established permissions. In discussing confidentiality, Steenhuis distinguishes subscription-based ChatGPT with history disabled and API systems from free ChatGPT under his account of policies at that time. Gilchrist's simplification recommendation explicitly excludes disclosure of client information.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The central affected groups are people with unmet civil legal needs, self-represented litigants, legal aid staff and organizations, and developers of legal self-help tools.
pts.d: Gilchrist focuses on North Carolina legal aid applicants facing delays or difficulty finding relevant help: AI could redirect ineligible applicants, accelerate intake and make dense website information easier to navigate. Steenhuis's guided-interview proposals concern self-represented users, including people facing eviction, who need to communicate their story and complete legal documents without repetitive questioning. Malloy describes renters with security-deposit problems and survivors needing to assert housing rights as examples of people who might benefit from differently calibrated conversational support. Clients with distressing circumstances may be excluded by moderation filters, while people with limited connectivity face access barriers that AI alone does not remove. Legal aid lawyers and staff could gain assistance with drafting code, editing communications, simplifying language and translation. Resource-constrained legal aid organizations may need partnerships to avoid falling behind; paywalls and engineering demands can impede deployment of vetted public-facing tools. Gilchrist says client communities already use generative AI and therefore need education to avoid harmful reliance when preparing their own pleadings. Steenhuis argues that excessive restrictions on vetted services could leave those clients using less safe alternatives. The discussion concerns access to justice and legal aid delivery, not enterprise purchasing, law-firm staffing ratios or quantified lawyer displacement.
